title: BOAC 781
summary: BOAC Flight 781, a De Havilland Comet jet, crashed on January 10, 1954, following an explosive decompression at altitude. The aircraft had departed Rome on the final leg to London when, at approximately 10:50, the cabin explosively depressurized and the fuselage broke apart, with debris falling into the sea near Elba, Italy. Investigation revealed the failure initiated in the roof of the cabin, propagating through the fuselage, with the tail section failing and outer wing structure collapsing. This was the second of three fatal Comet structural failures within twelve months, indicating systematic design or manufacturing vulnerabilities.
probable_cause: Structural failure of the fuselage due to metal fatigue cracks initiating in the cabin roof, propagating through the pressure bulkhead, leading to explosive decompression.

factors.evidence: fractures started in the roof of the cabin

the possibility of failure of the pressure cabin was also considered, but this theory was discounted because the Comet's cabin had been designed to a considerably higher strength than was considered necessary at the time
the same team of engineers examined this aircraft before its final flight and later examined South African Airways Flight 201 before its fatal flight
the possibility of failure of the pressure cabin was discounted
ruptured lungs were a sure indicator that the air cabin had depressurised

notes: part of larger de Havilland Comet accident series

title: 1954 BOAC Lockheed Constellation crash
summary: The aircraft struck a seawall while approaching Kallang Airport, damaging the undercarriage. On second touchdown the undercarriage collapsed and the starboard wing broke off as the aircraft slid, with the fuselage breaking in two. A post-impact fire killed most occupants; the jammed cabin door prevented evacuation. Investigation found the captain had been on duty for over 21 hours.
probable_cause: The captain was fatigued after being on duty for over 21 hours, which contributed to the approach error that led to striking the seawall.

title: South African Airways 201
summary: Jet airliner climbed rapidly from Rome toward cruising altitude of 35,000 feet. At 19:07 UTC aircraft contacted Cairo and reported estimated time of arrival. Shortly after at approximately 35,000 feet during climb the aircraft disintegrated in flight. All 21 occupants killed. Multi-year investigation chaired by Lionel Cohen revealed metal fatigue cracks in fuselage and manufacturer design defects in pressure boundary resulting in explosive decompression.
probable_cause: Manufacturer design defects and metal fatigue resulting in explosive decompression of the fuselage at altitude.

factors.evidence: official investigation revealed metal fatigue cracks that led to failure

events.text: At 18:32 UTC on Wednesday 7 April 1954 the aircraft took off from London for Rome.
At 19:07 UTC at approximately 35000 feet the aircraft contacted Cairo on the long range HF radio and reported an estimated time of arrival of 21:02 UTC.
At approximately 35000 feet the aircraft disintegrated from explosive decompression resulting from metal fatigue cracks and design defects in the pressure bulkhead.

notes: official investigation explicitly identified metal fatigue and design defects

investigation was extensive multi-year effort chaired by Lionel Cohen

title: Trans-Canada Air Lines 9
summary: Flight 9 departed Winnipeg at 08:58 in clear weather, climbed to 6000 feet. Harvard trainer departed RCAF Station Moose Jaw at 09:57 climbing to 9000 feet. At 10:02 as the Harvard reached 6000 feet, it collided with the North Star at combined speed of 261 knots. Both aircraft crashed. A large section of the North Star fell on a home in Moose Jaw.
probable_cause: Both aircrews failed to see and avoid each other. The Harvard was obscured from the North Star crew's view by a window post in their line of sight.

title: 1954 Cathay Pacific Douglas DC-4 shootdown
summary: Two PLA Air Force Lavochkin La-11 fighters attacked Cathay Pacific DC-4 VR-HEU while it cruised at 9,000 feet off Hainan Island. The fighters hit both outboard engines and damaged the rudder and aileron. Captain Phil Blown evaded the attack but lost control authority and ditched the aircraft in rough seas with 15-foot waves. The fuselage broke in two on impact, but survivors were rescued by Dutch and American vessels.
probable_cause: Military attack by PLA Air Force fighters on a civilian aircraft during the early Cold War period resulted in catastrophic structural and engine damage necessitating a ditching.

title: KLM 608
summary: KLM Flight 608 departed Shannon on 23 August 1954 for Amsterdam. The aircraft was flying in poor weather conditions with low clouds and heavy rain. After being cleared to descend to 2500 feet at 11:35, the aircraft did not respond to radio calls. Floating debris was found at 16:10 in the North Sea off the Dutch coast, but the cause of the crash was never determined.

title: KLM 633
summary: A Lockheed Super Constellation ditched in the River Shannon estuary shortly after takeoff from Shannon. The landing gear unexpectedly re-extended, causing the pilot to reduce power and descend to touch down in the estuary. The aircraft broke into two sections on impact. Fuel fumes from a ruptured tank rendered many unconscious, who then drowned in rising tide as rescue was delayed.
probable_cause: The aircraft descended to ditch due to unexpected re-extension of the landing gear and the captain's incorrect response to this situation. The official investigation concluded the accident was caused by an unexpected re-extension of the landing gear and the captain's incorrect behaviour.
